section.title: Java Core — JVM, Types & Syntax
section.subtitle: JDK/JRE/JVM, memory areas, garbage collection, data types, type conversion, operators, strings, arrays, comments, exceptions and more.

topics.title: JDK, JRE & JVM
topics.learn: What JDK, JRE and JVM are and how Java code runs.

python.definition: Python has no JVM. The Python interpreter reads .py files directly (or compiles to .pyc bytecode). You install one 'python' package — that's it.
python.code:
# Python: interpreter executes source directly
python3 script.py

# CPython compiles to bytecode in __pycache__/
# No separate JDK/JRE/JVM concept

java.definition: JDK = development kit (compiler javac + tools). JRE = runtime (JVM + libraries, runs compiled code). JVM = virtual machine that executes bytecode (.class). javac compiles .java -> .class, java runs it.

topics.title: Memory Areas & Garbage Collection
topics.learn: Static/dynamic memory, JVM memory regions, and how GC works (mark-sweep-compact).

python.definition: Python objects live on the heap, managed by CPython's reference counting + cyclic GC. No manual memory management; 'static' doesn't exist the same way.
python.code:
import gc

x = [1, 2, 3]      # heap object
del x               # refcount -> 0, freed (maybe)
gc.collect()        # force cyclic GC
print(gc.get_count())

java.definition: JVM memory: Method Area (class metadata), Heap (objects — dynamic), Stack (per-thread method calls), PC Register, Native Method Stack. GC algorithms: Mark-Sweep (mark live, sweep dead), Mark-Sweep-Compact (also defragments).

topics.title: Data Types & Memory Sizes
topics.learn: Primitive vs non-primitive types and how many bytes each takes.

python.definition: Everything is an object. int/float are arbitrary precision (no fixed size). sys.getsizeof() shows bytes. bool, str, list, dict, tuple, set are the built-ins.
python.code:
import sys

print(sys.getsizeof(10))        # 28 bytes (small int, cached)
print(sys.getsizeof(10**30))   # ~36 bytes (big int)
print(sys.getsizeof(3.14))     # 24 bytes (float)
print(sys.getsizeof("hi"))    # 50 bytes (str object)
print(sys.getsizeof([1,2,3]))   # 88 bytes + elements

# type check
print(type(10), type("x"), type([1]))

java.definition: Primitives have FIXED sizes: byte=1, short=2, char=2, int=4, long=8, float=4, double=8, boolean=1 (theoretical). Non-primitives (String, arrays, objects) live on heap. Check type with instanceof.
java.code:
// Sizes: byte 1 | short 2 | char 2 | int 4 | long 8 | float 4 | double 8
int i = 10;            // 4 bytes
long big = 10L;        // 8 bytes
double d = 3.14;       // 8 bytes

Object obj = "hi";   // heap reference
System.out.println(obj instanceof String); // true

// Check exact type
if (obj.getClass() == String.class) ...

topics.title: Type Conversion, Casting & Boxing
topics.learn: Primitive widening, upcasting/downcasting, automatic type promotion, boxing/unboxing.

python.definition: Python is dynamically typed — no casting needed, any variable holds any type. int()/float()/str() convert explicitly. No primitive/wrapper split.
python.code:
x = 10          # int
x = "hello"    # now str — totally fine

# Explicit conversion
a = int("42")
b = float(a)
c = str(b)

# Duck typing: just use it
print(len("abc"))     # works on str
# print(len(10))        # TypeError — no len() for int

java.definition: Widening (implicit): byte->short->int->long->float->double. Narrowing needs cast. Upcasting: subclass->superclass (safe). Downcasting: needs explicit cast + instanceof check. Boxing: int->Integer; unboxing: Integer->int (autoboxing is automatic).

topics.title: Operators — Unary, Ternary, Switch & Precedence
topics.learn: All operator types including BODMAS/precedence order.

python.definition: Unary: -x, not x, +x. Ternary: a if cond else b. switch statement (3.10+): match/case. Precedence (high->low): (), [], {}, **, unary, *,/,//,%, +,-, shifts, &, ^, |, comparisons, not, and, or.
python.code:
x = 5
print(-x, not False)                    # unary

# Ternary
status = "adult" if x >= 18 else "minor"

# Precedence demo (BODMAS)
print(2 + 3 * 4)          # 14 — * before +
print((2 + 3) * 4)        # 20 — parens first
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)        # 512 — ** right-assoc

# Switch (3.10+)
match x:
    case 1: print("one")
    case _: print("other")

java.definition: Unary: -x, !x, ++x. Ternary: cond ? a : b. switch expression with -> and yield (Java 14+). Precedence: (), [], ., unary, */%, +-, shifts, relational, ==/!=, &, ^, |, &&, ||, ternary, assignment.

topics.title: String Pool & Immutability
topics.learn: How strings are stored, why String is immutable, StringBuilder vs StringBuffer.

python.definition: Python interns some strings automatically. Strings are immutable — every 'change' creates a new object. No StringBuilder; use ''.join() or f-strings for building.
python.code:
a = "hello"
b = "hello"
print(a is b)          # True — interned!

c = "hello " + "world"   # new object

# Build strings efficiently
parts = [str(i) for i in range(1000)]
s = "".join(parts)         # fast — join once

java.definition: String literals go to the String Pool — identical literals share one object. new String() forces heap copy. Immutability = thread-safe + cacheable hashCode. StringBuilder = fast mutable (not thread-safe); StringBuffer = synchronized version.

topics.title: String Methods — Both Languages
topics.learn: Common string operations side by side.

python.definition: Python string methods return NEW strings (immutable). Key methods: lower, upper, strip, split, join, replace, find/index, startswith, count, format.
python.code:
s = "  Hello World  "

s.lower()          # '  hello world  '
s.upper()          # '  HELLO WORLD  '
s.strip()          # 'Hello World'
s.split()          # ['Hello', 'World']
s.replace('World','Py')
s.find('World')    # index or -1
s.startswith('Hel')
','.join(['a','b']) # 'a,b'

# char access
s[0]               # 'H'
len(s)             # length

java.definition: Java String methods also return new Strings. Key methods: toLowerCase, toUpperCase, trim/strip, split, String.join, replace, indexOf, startsWith, formatted/format.
java.code:
String s = "  Hello World  ";

s.toLowerCase()    // "  hello world  "
s.toUpperCase()    // "  HELLO WORLD  "
s.trim()           // "Hello World"
s.split(" ")       // [Hello, World]
s.replace("World","Java")
s.indexOf("World")  // index or -1
s.startsWith("Hel")
String.join(",", "a","b") // "a,b"

s.charAt(0)        // 'H'
s.length()         // length
s.isEmpty()        // boolean

topics.title: Character Methods & Unicode
topics.learn: Working with individual characters and Unicode ranges.

python.definition: Python strings are Unicode by default. ord() -> code point, chr() -> char. str.isalpha(), isdigit(), isalnum() classify characters.
python.code:
ch = 'A'
print(ord(ch))        # 65 (ASCII)
print(chr(66))       # 'B'
print('€'.encode())  # b'\xe2\x82\xac' UTF-8

for c in 'aB3!':
    print(c, c.isalpha(), c.isdigit(), c.isalnum())
# 'a' True False True
# '3' False True True
# '!' False False False

java.definition: char = 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. Character class has static methods: isLetter, isDigit, isLetterOrDigit, isUpperCase, toLowerCase. Unicode escapes: \u0041 = 'A'.

topics.title: Creating Arrays — Both Languages
topics.learn: Array declaration, types of arrays (1D, 2D, jagged).

python.definition: Python has no fixed arrays — lists serve that role. Nested lists = 2D arrays; lists of different lengths = jagged. NumPy for real arrays.
python.code:
# 1D
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4]

# 2D (matrix)
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(matrix[1][2])     # 6

# Jagged (rows of different length)
jagged = [[1, 2], [3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(jagged[2][1])     # 5

# NumPy real arrays
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1,2],[3,4]])
print(a.shape)          # (2, 2) fixed-size

java.definition: Arrays are fixed-size, typed objects. 1D: int[]. 2D: int[][]. Jagged: rows can differ. Length via .length. Enhanced for-loop iterates.

python.definition: # single-line. """docstring""" = documentation (module/class/function doc). No true block comment — consecutive # lines used.
python.code:
# Single line comment
x = 10  # inline comment

"""Module docstring — describes this file."""

def add(a, b):
    """Function docstring — shown by help(add)."""
    return a + b

# Multi-line = just multiple # lines
# line 1
# line 2

java.definition: // single-line, /* */ multi-line block, /** */ Javadoc documentation (generates API docs).

python.definition: Python has no ++ operator — use += 1 / -= 1. No pre/post distinction exists.
python.code:
a = 5
a += 1        # same as a++ in Java
a -= 1        # same as a--

# No ++a or a++ in Python — SyntaxError
# b = a++ would fail

java.definition: ++a (pre): increment FIRST, then use new value. a++ (post): use OLD value, then increment. -- works the same downward.
java.code:
int a = 5;
System.out.println(a++);   // prints 5, a becomes 6
System.out.println(++a);   // a becomes 7, prints 7
System.out.println(a--);   // prints 7, a becomes 6
System.out.println(--a);   // a becomes 5, prints 5

// Compound assignment (equivalent)
int b = a; a += 1;   // like post-increment
int c = (a += 1);   // like pre-increment

topics.title: Constructors & this/super Keywords
topics.learn: Default vs explicit constructors; this and super.

python.definition: __init__ is the constructor — runs on object creation. self = this (current instance). super() calls parent constructor/method. No default constructor concept — __init__ always exists.

java.definition: Constructor = method named after class, no return type. Default ctor auto-created if none defined. this = current instance; super = parent class. super() must be first statement.

topics.title: Static & Instance Blocks
topics.learn: Initialization blocks that run at class load / object creation.

python.definition: No static/instance blocks. Class-level code runs at definition time; __init__ runs per instance; __new__ before __init__.

java.definition: static {} block runs ONCE when class loads (before any object). Instance {} block runs before constructor on EVERY new object. Order: static block -> instance block -> constructor.

topics.title: Access Modifiers
topics.learn: public, protected, private, default — controlling visibility.

python.definition: No access modifiers — everything is public by convention. _name = 'internal use', __name = name-mangled 'private-ish'. __all__ controls import *.
python.code:
class Bank:
    def __init__(self):
        self.public = 1        # accessible anywhere
        self._protected = 2     # convention: internal
        self.__private = 3      # name-mangled -> _Bank__private

b = Bank()
print(b.public, b._protected)
print(b._Bank__private)   # can still reach it (no real privacy)

java.definition: private = class only; default (no modifier) = same package; protected = package + subclasses; public = everywhere. Enforced at compile time.

topics.title: POJO Classes & Serialization
topics.learn: Plain Old Java Objects and saving objects to files/streams.

python.definition: Any class instance can be pickled (serialized) with pickle module — converts object to bytes for storage/network. __dict__ holds attributes.
python.code:
import pickle

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

s = Student("Priya", 20)

# Serialize -> bytes/file
with open("student.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump(s, f)

# Deserialize
with open("student.pkl", "rb") as f:
    s2 = pickle.load(f)
print(s2.name, s2.age)

java.definition: POJO = plain class: private fields, public getters/setters, no-arg ctor, implements Serializable for object->byte[] conversion (ObjectOutputStream).

topics.title: Exceptions — try/catch/throws/throw/finally/finalize
topics.learn: Full exception handling including checked vs unchecked, stack traces, and deprecated finalize().

python.definition: try/except/else/finally. raise throws, except catches. All exceptions inherit Exception — no checked/unchecked split (though some like KeyboardInterrupt inherit BaseException). __del__ ~ finalize (deprecated).

java.definition: try/catch/finally; throw throws an exception object; throws declares checked exceptions a method may raise. Checked (IOException) MUST be handled; unchecked (RuntimeException) optional. printStackTrace() prints trace; finalize() deprecated -> try-with-resources.
